description: Spring & Spring Boot : fondamentaux, IoC/DI, beans & annotations, REST/MVC, validation, exceptions, Spring Data JPA/Hibernate, Spring Security (JWT) et sujets avancés (@Transactional, email SMTP, CORS…) avec exemples de code.

questions.prompt: What is Spring Boot and what are its advantages?
questions.answer_text:
Spring Boot is a Spring-based Java framework that lets you create stand-alone, production-ready applications with minimal configuration.
- Stand-alone: runs without an external server (java -jar app.jar) via an embedded Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow server, on port 8080 by default.
- Auto-configuration: configures the app automatically based on the dependencies on the classpath.
- Production-ready: built-in metrics, health checks, monitoring (Actuator), logging, external configuration.
- Easy dependency management with starters.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between Spring and Spring Boot?
questions.answer_text:
Spring is the base Java framework (dependency injection, MVC, data access, security) but requires an external server and manual XML/Java configuration.
Spring Boot is a layer on top of Spring that simplifies development with auto-configuration, embedded servers, and starter dependencies. Spring needs more manual setup; Spring Boot reduces boilerplate and makes apps easier to build and run.

questions.prompt: Explain the evolution: Java SE → Java EE → Spring → Spring Boot.
questions.answer_text: Java EE is the official Java enterprise standard (APIs like JPA, JMS, Servlets), usually running on heavy application servers. Spring is a lightweight, modular framework that provides the same features more simply, which made it more popular than Java EE. Spring Boot builds on Spring to remove most configuration.

questions.prompt: Explain the @SpringBootApplication annotation.
questions.answer_text:
@SpringBootApplication is the core annotation of Spring Boot. It combines three annotations:
- @Configuration: for bean configuration.
- @EnableAutoConfiguration: for classpath-based auto-configuration.
- @ComponentScan: for auto-discovery of components (@Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller).
Spring scans the package of the main class and all its subpackages.

questions.prompt: What is auto-configuration in Spring Boot?
questions.answer_text: Auto-configuration works with @EnableAutoConfiguration (part of @SpringBootApplication). Spring Boot automatically configures things based on the dependencies you add. For example, spring-boot-starter-web auto-configures an embedded Tomcat and the DispatcherServlet; spring-boot-starter-data-jpa configures the DB connection and JPA repositories. This saves a lot of manual configuration.

questions.prompt: Explain 'Convention over Configuration'.
questions.answer_text: It means Spring Boot provides predefined rules and automatic setup, so you don't write much configuration as long as you follow its recommended patterns. Example: the class annotated with @SpringBootApplication in com.example.app makes Spring automatically scan that package and its subpackages for beans — you don't need to declare @ComponentScan manually.

questions.prompt: What is a Spring Boot starter?
questions.answer_text:
A starter is a pre-configured set of dependencies for a specific feature, letting you add functionality quickly without configuring each library. Examples:
- spring-boot-starter-web → Spring MVC, JSON support, embedded server.
- spring-boot-starter-data-jpa → JPA/Hibernate and DB access.
- spring-boot-starter-security → authentication/authorization.
- spring-boot-starter-test → JUnit, Mockito, etc.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of application.properties / application.yml?
questions.answer_text: They configure the external settings of a Spring Boot app (database connection, server port, logging, environment-specific properties) without hardcoding them in the source. application.properties uses key-value pairs; application.yml uses a hierarchical format that is more readable for complex configuration.

questions.prompt: What is Spring Initializr?
questions.answer_text: Spring Initializr (https://start.spring.io) is a web tool to generate a Spring Boot project skeleton with the dependencies you select.

questions.prompt: What is a Bean and what are the steps to create it?
questions.answer_text:
A bean is an object automatically managed by Spring. It's created via component scanning and annotations like @Service, @Repository, @Component, @Controller.
Steps: 1) annotate your class (@Service, @Component…); 2) Spring scans the configured packages (or via @SpringBootApplication); 3) it detects the class and creates it as a bean; 4) the bean is added to the Spring container (ApplicationContext); 5) you inject it elsewhere with @Autowired or @Inject.

questions.prompt: What is IoC (Inversion of Control) and the ApplicationContext?
questions.answer_text: IoC is a design principle: instead of objects creating their own dependencies, a container creates and wires them. The IoC container in Spring creates and manages beans and handles dependency injection. ApplicationContext is the implementation of this principle — the container where all beans are created, stored, and injected where needed.

questions.prompt: What is dependency injection (DI) and its types?
questions.answer_text:
DI is a design pattern where a class receives its dependencies from the outside instead of creating them itself. It's the core of Spring.
Types:
- Constructor injection (recommended) — @RequiredArgsConstructor auto-generates a constructor with all final/@NonNull fields.
- Setter injection.
- Field injection (not recommended).

questions.prompt: Field Injection vs Constructor Injection: which is better and why?
questions.answer_text: Constructor injection is recommended: dependencies can be final (immutable), the object is always created in a valid state, it's easier to test (you pass mocks via the constructor), and it avoids hidden dependencies. Field injection (@Autowired on a field) is discouraged: harder to test, can't be final, and hides dependencies. @RequiredArgsConstructor (Lombok) generates the constructor automatically.

questions.prompt: How does @Autowired work (and why doesn't it work on static fields)?
questions.answer_text: @Autowired asks Spring to inject an already-created bean from the container into another class. Spring manages beans (instances), not static classes — it injects into instance fields, not static fields. To use an injected dependency in a static context, use a non-static setter annotated with @Autowired that assigns the value to a static field; without @Autowired, Spring never calls it and the field stays null (NullPointerException).

questions.prompt: What is the difference between @Autowired and @Inject?
questions.answer_text: @Autowired is Spring-specific and allows extra options like required=false. @Inject is a standard Java (JSR-330) annotation, more generic and portable, but with fewer options.

questions.prompt: Difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller and @RestController?
questions.answer_text:
All are specializations of @Component (so all become Spring beans); they add semantic meaning per layer:
- @Component: generic bean.
- @Service: business-logic layer.
- @Repository: data-access (DAO) layer, with exception translation.
- @Controller: web layer returning views (JSP/Thymeleaf), traditional MVC.
- @RestController (= @Controller + @ResponseBody): REST APIs; handles HTTP requests and returns JSON/XML.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between @Configuration and @Component?
questions.answer_text: @Component makes the class itself a bean (detected via scanning). @Configuration declares a configuration class where @Bean-annotated methods manually create beans — it's not the whole class that becomes a bean, but the objects returned by the @Bean methods.

questions.prompt: What are @Qualifier and @Primary?
questions.answer_text:
Both resolve ambiguity when several beans of the same type exist.
- @Qualifier: used with @Autowired to specify exactly which bean to inject.
- @Primary: marks the default bean to inject when multiple exist — then @Qualifier is not needed for that 'main' bean.

questions.prompt: What are @Value, @Profile and @ConfigurationProperties?
questions.answer_text:
- @Value: injects values into beans from configuration files, environment variables, or expressions.
- @Profile: defines beans that are loaded only for specific environments/profiles (dev, test, prod).
- @ConfigurationProperties: binds a group of external properties to a typed configuration object.

questions.prompt: How do you create a REST API with Spring Boot?
questions.answer_text: Define a model class (@Entity), a repository interface (@Repository / extends JpaRepository), a service class (@Service) for business logic, and a controller (@RestController) handling HTTP requests with @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping. Spring Boot handles dependency injection and runs the app on an embedded server.

questions.prompt: Explain @RequestMapping, @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, @DeleteMapping.
questions.answer_text:
- @RequestMapping: defines the base path for all controller methods.
- @GetMapping: read/retrieve data (GET).
- @PostMapping: create a new resource (POST).
- @PutMapping: fully update a resource (PUT).
- @PatchMapping: partially update a resource (PATCH).
- @DeleteMapping: delete a resource (DELETE).

questions.prompt: What Spring annotations extract data from an HTTP request (@PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody, @RequestHeader, @CookieValue, @ModelAttribute)?
questions.answer_text:
- @PathVariable: part of the URL path (/users/42) — identify a resource.
- @RequestParam: query-string value (/users?name=Ali) — filters, pagination, sorting.
- @RequestBody: HTTP request body (JSON/XML) → Java object — create/update.
- @RequestHeader: HTTP headers (User-Agent, Authorization).
- @CookieValue: HTTP cookies (@CookieValue("JSESSIONID")).
- @ModelAttribute: form data (x-www-form-urlencoded) bound to a Java object.
- @MatrixVariable: variables in the path with ; (rarely used).

questions.prompt: What are ResponseEntity and @ResponseBody?
questions.answer_text:
@ResponseBody tells Spring the method's return value goes directly into the HTTP response body (often converted to JSON via Jackson). It's implicit in @RestController.
ResponseEntity is a class (not an annotation) representing a full HTTP response: body + status code + headers → more control. Factory methods: ResponseEntity.ok(body), ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus).body(x), ResponseEntity.badRequest(), ResponseEntity.notFound().build(), ResponseEntity.noContent().build(), ResponseEntity.created(uri).

questions.prompt: What are the common HTTP status codes?
questions.answer_text:
- 200 OK: success with data.
- 201 Created: resource created (POST).
- 204 No Content: success with nothing to return.
- 400 Bad Request: bad client request.
- 401 Unauthorized: not authenticated.
- 403 Forbidden: access denied.
- 404 Not Found: resource not found.
- 422 Unprocessable Entity: valid format but logically inconsistent.
- 500 Internal Server Error: server-side error.

questions.prompt: What is CORS and the @CrossOrigin annotation?
questions.answer_text:
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a security mechanism that allows a server's resources to be shared across different origins (domains/ports). @CrossOrigin enables CORS for a controller or method, allowing your API to be called from web apps on other domains (e.g. a front-end on localhost:3000 calling an API on localhost:8080). Without it, browsers block cross-origin requests.
⚠️ @CrossOrigin(origins = "*") is fine in development but dangerous in production — restrict it to your front-end origin (e.g. https://mon-site.com).

questions.prompt: What is the difference between @Valid and @Validated?
questions.answer_text:
- @Validated: placed on the controller/service class; enables validation of method parameters (e.g. @PathVariable, @RequestParam) and annotations like @Email, @Pattern on parameters.
- @Valid: placed on method parameters (typically DTO objects received via @RequestBody); triggers validation of the object's fields based on the DTO's annotations (@NotNull, @Size, etc.).
Common validation annotations: @NotNull, @NotEmpty, @NotBlank, @Size, @Email, @Pattern, @Min, @Max.

questions.prompt: What is @ExceptionHandler and @RestControllerAdvice?
questions.answer_text:
@ExceptionHandler catches and handles exceptions thrown in controller methods (in a controller or in a @RestControllerAdvice).
@RestControllerAdvice = @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody: it defines global exception handlers for all REST controllers and returns responses in JSON. Benefits: centralizes error handling, avoids repeated try-catch, and gives uniform error responses.

questions.prompt: What is the Environment class in Spring?
questions.answer_text: The Environment class represents the application's runtime environment. It's mainly used to access configuration properties — values defined in application.properties, application.yml, system environment variables, and command-line arguments.

questions.prompt: What is Spring Boot Actuator?
questions.answer_text:
Actuator provides ready-to-use endpoints to monitor and manage an application:
- health → application health status.
- metrics → CPU, memory, requests.
- info → application info.
- env → environment variables.
- beans → list of beans in the Spring context.

questions.prompt: What is a layered architecture in Spring Boot?
questions.answer_text:
- View: user interface (JSP, HTML, React…).
- Controller: handles HTTP requests and calls services.
- DTO: simple objects to transfer data between layers (lighter and safer than entities, no JPA annotations).
- Service: business logic (processing, validation, conversions) and calls repositories.
- Repository: data access (CRUD via Spring Data JPA).
- Entity/Model: classes mapped to database tables.
- Database: stores the data.

questions.prompt: What is Thymeleaf?
questions.answer_text: Thymeleaf is a server-side template engine used with Spring Boot to generate dynamic HTML pages. It mixes HTML with Spring model data using attributes like th:text and th:each. It's used in Spring MVC apps that render views (without React/Angular).

questions.prompt: What is ORM, JPA, Hibernate, and Spring Data JPA (how do they relate)?
questions.answer_text:
- ORM (Object Relational Mapping): a technique to map Java objects to database tables so you work with objects instead of SQL.
- JPA (Java Persistence API): a specification (interface/standard) defining how ORM should be done in Java (annotations @Entity, @Id; the EntityManager interface). It has no implementation itself.
- Hibernate: the most popular concrete implementation of JPA — the underlying engine that runs the SQL. It adds extras (HQL, second-level cache).
- Spring Data JPA: an abstraction on top of JPA (and Hibernate) that reduces boilerplate — it auto-generates repository implementations from interfaces (e.g. findByLastName(String)).

questions.prompt: What is the difference between JPA and Hibernate?
questions.answer_text: JPA is the specification (the contract/interface). Hibernate is an implementation (the framework that implements the contract and actually executes SQL).

questions.prompt: What are the main JPA annotations (@Entity, @Id, @GeneratedValue, @Column…)?
questions.answer_text:
- @Entity: marks a class as a JPA entity (linked to a table).
- @Table(name = "users"): specifies the table name (optional).
- @Id: the entity's primary key.
- @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY): auto-generates the primary key (IDENTITY, AUTO, SEQUENCE, TABLE).
- @Column(name, nullable, length…): customizes the column.
- @Transient: excludes a field from persistence.
- @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING): stores an enum as text.
- @Lob: for large fields (long text, BLOB).

questions.prompt: What are the JPA relationships?
questions.answer_text: @OneToOne (one-to-one), @OneToMany (one-to-many), @ManyToOne (many-to-one), @ManyToMany (many-to-many).

questions.prompt: What is the JPA entity lifecycle?
questions.answer_text:
- Transient: a new Java object, not yet persisted.
- Managed: tracked by the EntityManager (changes synchronized with the DB).
- Detached: no longer tracked (after close(), clear(), or leaving scope).
- Removed: marked for deletion.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between persist() and merge()?
questions.answer_text: persist() saves a new entity and makes it managed by the persistence context. merge() updates a detached entity and returns a new managed copy (the original object stays detached).

questions.prompt: What is JPQL?
questions.answer_text: JPQL (Java Persistence Query Language) is an object-oriented query language used with JPA. It's similar to SQL but works on entities and their attributes, not directly on tables/columns, and is database-independent (Hibernate translates JPQL into native SQL for the target DBMS).

questions.prompt: What is @Query in Spring Data JPA?
questions.answer_text: @Query is a Spring Data JPA annotation that lets you write a custom query (JPQL or native SQL) directly in the repository, instead of relying on derived methods like findByName().

questions.prompt: What is lazy loading vs eager loading?
questions.answer_text: Lazy loading loads related entities only when they are accessed (on demand). Eager loading loads them immediately together with the main entity. Relationships (@OneToMany, @ManyToOne…) can be configured with FetchType.LAZY or FetchType.EAGER.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between save() and saveAndFlush()?
questions.answer_text: save() saves an entity into the persistence context, but the SQL execution can be delayed until the transaction commits. saveAndFlush() does the same but forces a flush, writing changes to the database immediately.

questions.prompt: In Hibernate, what is the difference between get() and load()?
questions.answer_text: get() hits the database immediately and returns the real object, or null if not found. load() returns a proxy (ghost object) and fetches data lazily; if the entity doesn't exist, it throws an exception (ObjectNotFoundException).

questions.prompt: How do you configure a database with Spring Boot?
questions.answer_text:
In application.properties/yml, define e.g.:
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/mydb
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=1234
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.dialect=org.hibernate.dialect.MySQL8Dialect
Spring Boot auto-configures the DataSource, EntityManager, and transaction manager.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between CrudRepository and JpaRepository?
questions.answer_text: JpaRepository = CrudRepository + additional JPA/Hibernate features (batch operations, pagination and sorting via PagingAndSortingRepository, flushing, etc.). Spring Data auto-implements the interface at runtime.

questions.prompt: What is @Transactional?
questions.answer_text: @Transactional tells Spring the method must run inside a transaction — a set of operations that must all succeed or all fail together. If everything succeeds, Spring commits (changes saved); if an error occurs, Spring rolls back (all changes undone). Rule of thumb: any method that writes to the DB and may be part of a larger operation should be @Transactional, so multiple updates can be combined into one atomic transaction.

questions.prompt: What are common MongoDB update operators (with Spring)?
questions.answer_text:
MongoDB update operators used with MongoOperations/MongoTemplate:
- $inc → increment/decrement a field.
- $set → replace a field's value.
- $addToSet → add to an array without duplicates.
- $pull → remove an element from an array.

questions.prompt: What is Authentication vs Authorization in Spring Security?
questions.answer_text: Authentication verifies the user's identity (who you are — login). Authorization verifies the user's permissions/roles (what you're allowed to do).

questions.prompt: What are UserDetails, UserDetailsService and PasswordEncoder in Spring Security?
questions.answer_text:
- UserDetails: an interface representing an authenticated user (username, password, authorities/roles, account enabled or not).
- UserDetailsService: an interface that lets Spring Security load the user from the database.
- PasswordEncoder: hashes the password before storing it (e.g. BCryptPasswordEncoder).

questions.prompt: How does JWT authentication work in Spring Security?
questions.answer_text:
JWT (JSON Web Token) is a secure token issued by the server after login. Flow:
1) User logs in (username + password).
2) Server returns a JWT.
3) Client sends the JWT in every request (Authorization: Bearer …).
4) Server validates the token.
A filter (extending OncePerRequestFilter) intercepts each HTTP request to read the JWT, verify its validity, and authenticate the user.

questions.prompt: What are @EnableWebSecurity, SecurityFilterChain, @PreAuthorize and @Secured?
questions.answer_text:
- @EnableWebSecurity: activates Spring Security in the application.
- SecurityFilterChain: defines the security rules for HTTP requests (which endpoints are public/protected, filters…).
- @PreAuthorize: checks the user's rights before a method executes (e.g. @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")).
- @Secured: restricts access to a method based on the user's role.

questions.prompt: How do you send an OTP email via SMTP in Spring Boot?
questions.answer_text:
1) Add the mail dependency (spring-boot-starter-mail) via Spring Initializr.
2) Configure the SMTP properties in application.properties (spring.mail.host, port, username, password, properties.mail.smtp.auth/starttls).
3) Create the mail service using JavaMailSender (build a MimeMessage with subject and HTML body).
4) Add a utility method to generate the OTP code.
5) A service method sendOtp(...) builds and sends the email.
6) Expose it via a controller endpoint.
(The attached screenshots show the properties, the classes, the HTML OTP template, the code generator, the sendOtp method, and the controller.)

questions.prompt: What is @EnableScheduling and scheduled tasks?
questions.answer_text: @EnableScheduling activates Spring's scheduling support. You can then annotate methods with @Scheduled (fixedRate, fixedDelay, or cron) to run recurring background tasks automatically (e.g. cleanup jobs, sending reminders).

questions.prompt: What is the Spring bean lifecycle?
questions.answer_text: The bean lifecycle starts when Spring creates the bean instance, injects its dependencies, and runs initialization methods (e.g. @PostConstruct / afterPropertiesSet). The bean is then ready to use. When the application context shuts down, Spring calls the destroy methods (@PreDestroy / destroy) to clean up resources.

questions.prompt: What is @Override in Java?
questions.answer_text: @Override indicates that a method redefines (overrides) a method already declared in a parent class or interface. It makes the intent explicit and lets the compiler verify the signature is correct — if you get the name or parameters wrong, you get a compile error.

questions.prompt: What is a REST API and what is JSON?
questions.answer_text: A REST API is a type of API that uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to interact with data, usually in JSON format; it's widely used in web and mobile apps. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight, human-readable data-exchange format that machines parse easily — the common format for REST APIs.
